text: Ukrainian sources told The Telegraph in 2024 that Ukraine's acoustic air-surveillance project was "too secret to discuss in detail".

cites.quote: too secret to discuss in detail

text: Both the ePPO app and Ukraine's acoustic sensor networks were built in 2022 to fill radar's low-altitude blind zone, which the Earth's curvature and terrain create.
A Ukrainian defence outlet puts a typical radar's detection range against a target flying at 100 m altitude at 40–50 km, depending on terrain.

observations.subject: typical radar against a target at 100 m altitude

text: The ePPO app, launched on 13 October 2022 by the volunteer group Tekhnari, turns a phone into a sensor: when the user points it along the target's flight and presses one button it sends the phone's geolocation and compass heading, and reports can also be made from sound.
ePPO users log in through Diia "so that enemies and fools don't interfere with gunners with false targets".

cites.quote: so that enemies and fools don't interfere with gunners with false targets

text: According to Ukraine's deputy defence minister, an ePPO report reaches air-defence maps in 2–7 seconds.

ePPO's reported scale grew from 600,000 downloads and 200,000 active users in November 2024 to more than 850,000 verified users and more than 4 million reports in 2025–26 (the later figures secondary).
Successive reports put Ukraine's Sky Fortress acoustic network at about 6,000 nodes (February 2024), 8,000 (March 2024), 9,500 (July 2024) and 14,000 (July 2025), at about $400–1,000 a node.
Ukraine's separate Zvook acoustic network uses fewer, longer-range parabolic-mirror sensors on 10–12 m towers, and had 210 nodes covering about 5% of Ukraine in 2024.

metric_new.label: Share of an area covered by a sensor network

text: Zvook reports detection ranges of about 5 km for drones and 7 km for cruise missiles, with data in Delta within about 12 seconds (vendor claims).

Gen. James Hecker told in 2024 of an 84-drone raid in which fire teams using acoustic tracks downed 80 drones; it is repeated in every later source and is the only quantified field result for Ukraine's acoustic network.

observations.subject: drones in one raid tracked acoustically
drones downed by fire teams using acoustic tracks

text: United24 says about 20% of targets entering Ukraine are tracked by acoustic data alone.

observations.subject: targets entering Ukraine tracked by acoustics alone

metric_new.label: Share of targets tracked by acoustic sensors alone

text: From 2024–25 Russian Shaheds cruised above 2 km, where Ukrainian Air Force spokesman Yurii Ihnat said they are "more visible to our radars" but out of gun reach.
Other Russian Shaheds flew low, up to about 200 m, in radar blind spots, and decoys made up about 40% of waves (2024–25).
Russian decoys carry Luneburg lenses to look like Shaheds on radar, Ukrainian radars merge 3–4 close targets into one, and decoys that vanish are logged as "lost from location".

observations.subject: targets a radar merges into one plot

text: Oryx has visually confirmed 152 Ukrainian radars and communications systems lost, including 32 36D6 (16 "Tin Shield" and 16 ST-68U), 30 P-18-family, 2 TRML-4D (IRIS-T), 2 AN/MPQ-53 (Patriot) and 2 RADA ieMHR.
Russian decoys "identify positions" of Ukrainian air defence for later strikes, and from April 2026 guided Shaheds hunt the mobile fire groups that fire on them.
In early May 2022 Andriy Kosiak proposed the idea of ePPO, a prototype was written in days, and the volunteer group Tekhnari (about 10 people) merged with IT WAR UA.

From May to September 2022 ePPO's developers coordinated with Operational Command South, its air-defence command and the Navy's air defence; the APK was tested by "several hundred" trusted people and a beta came out about August.
ePPO was publicly launched on Google Play for Android on 13 October 2022, with iOS promised "soon".

ePPO's developers claim its first success on 22 October 2022: a Kalibr missing from radar because of terrain masking was shot down in southern Ukraine from citizen reports, with "four minutes" of warning.

observations.subject: warning of a Kalibr from ePPO reports

text: In the first week of Shahed waves in October 2022, Suldin of the ePPO team says that on one night 19 of 20 drones were shot down, and people who heard but did not see them helped "draw" their tracks.

observations.subject: Shahed drones shot down on one night

text: To make an ePPO report the user chooses the target type (drone, missile, aircraft, helicopter), points the phone in the direction the target is moving and presses a large red button.
An ePPO report sends the phone's geolocation and the heading from its compass; a developer said "Geolocation is the only data type the ePPO app asks from a person".

cites.quote: Geolocation is the only data type the ePPO app asks from a person

text: The 2022 ePPO instructions say to point the phone "in the direction the target is moving", while a 2024 account says users point it "at an approaching object"; the two descriptions differ, and no source says which one the server assumes.

cites.quote: in the direction the target is moving

text: Drones were reported in ePPO by people who heard but did not see them, and a 2026 account calls sound-based reports especially useful for Shahed-type drones.

ePPO reports are processed on a server and passed to the military, and the developers say geolocation is "not stored anywhere"; several reports along one path gave a commander enough points to direct a unit.

ePPO reports are aggregated in real time to estimate a target's direction and speed, and users along the predicted path get a warning about 10 minutes before overflight; public outputs show only location and type, and some data is restricted to military use.

observations.subject: ePPO warning to users before overflight

text: Deputy Defence Minister Kateryna Chernohorenko said in November 2024 that ePPO reports appear "on the air defense maps of all officers in 2–7 seconds".

cites.quote: on the air defense maps of all officers in 2–7 seconds

text: ePPO's developers called it "a supplementary detection system, not the primary one", and valued rural reports most: ten users among fishermen and farmers on the approach routes were worth more than a thousand in a big city.

cites.quote: ePPO is a supplementary detection system, not the primary one

text: Diia login was the stated defence of ePPO against false reports from the enemy and pranksters, and state IT bodies reviewed the app's code.

No fetched source describes ePPO duplicate merging, per-user trust scores, outlier rejection or a measured false-report rate; a 2026 Western analysis only warns in general terms of "data poisoning" sending interceptors to the wrong place, and recommends outlier analytics.

The only documented Russian attacks on ePPO's developers were DDoS attacks on IT WAR's services, with two short outages; the source does not say ePPO was among them, and no fetched source documents spoofed ePPO reports.

observations.subject: outages from DDoS attacks on IT WAR services

text: Deputy Defence Minister Kateryna Chernohorenko said ePPO users help "close Ukrainian airspace by 80%", giving no method.

observations.subject: airspace closed with the help of ePPO users

text: Thousands of Ukrainian volunteer air wardens, mostly retired military or local officials in villages, report aircraft seen or heard, with a direction, by phone, text or to the nearest unit.
By early 2024 national and local Telegram channels were the main real-time air-threat source for both the Ukrainian military and the public (Kyiv Post analysis).
Ukrainian early warning often comes hours before a strike, when Russian bombers fly to launch areas, and Russian crews have been seen loading launch racks in Crimea and southern Russia.
Ballistic warning is short: on 2 July 2026 the Ukrainian Air Force alert "two missiles from Kursk Oblast" (01:58) was followed by "approaching Kyiv" two minutes later.

observations.subject: from launch alert to approaching Kyiv

text: In 2026 Ukrainian mobile fire groups still learned of drones mainly by hearing them; warnings often came "when we already hear it".
An Igla operator says propeller Shaheds give warning by engine noise, while jet drones and cruise missiles can be almost overhead before they are heard.
In November 2024 ePPO had more than 600,000 downloads and about 200,000 active users, used AI to predict trajectories and sent users "It's coming at you" warnings.
By December 2025 ePPO had received more than 4 million reports in total, according to a secondary Western source citing the Snake Island Institute.
In 2026 ePPO had more than 850,000 Diia-verified users (secondary source).
ePPO's developers explained in 2022 that a missile at 800 km/h flies 200 m a second, so a minute's delay in a report means kilometres of error.

Russia's "Radar" app, developed by All-Russia People's Front activists and pushed to millions via the state portal on 20–21 September 2023, has a near-identical point-and-press interface to ePPO; its developers claimed 50,000+ downloads in a month and two drones downed over Bryansk Oblast.

observations.subject: drones downed over Bryansk Oblast with the Radar app

notes: Russian claim relayed from the Washington Post.

text: Sky Fortress (Skyfortress) was built by an anonymous NGO of Ukrainian engineers that is in the Brave1 pool, and Ajax Systems was named for a 12,500-sensor fundraising tranche.

observations.subject: Sky Fortress sensors in an Ajax Systems fundraising tranche

text: Zvook was built by Lviv volunteers whose founders include Respeecher co-founder Dmytro Bielievtsov, i3 Engineering CEO Pavlo Tsiupka and serviceman Marian Sulym.
Sky Fortress started in 2022 against low-flying cruise missiles; Zvook also started in 2022 and had more than 40 stations by December 2022.
A first-generation Sky Fortress node was an Android phone in a box on a pole about 6 ft (1.8 m) high, later replaced by a custom CPU and sound card.
A Zvook node is a microphone at the focus of a parabolic acoustic mirror, mounted on telecom towers at 10–12 m.

observations.subject: Zvook mounting height on telecom towers

text: Sky Fortress node counts were reported at about 6,000 (February 2024), 8,000 (March 2024), 9,500 (July 2024) and 14,000 (July 2025), and 15,000 third-generation nodes have been funded by NATO allies.

observations.subject: Sky Fortress third-generation nodes funded by NATO allies

text: Zvook grew from 40+ stations (December 2022) to 210 (March 2024); a figure of "nearly 300" later appears only in a search snippet.
A Sky Fortress node is reported to cost about $500, $400–500 or $400–1,000 depending on the source.
A Zvook node costs about £400 to make, or about $500.
Gen. James Hecker said the whole Sky Fortress network cost "less than two Patriot missiles"; an analyst range puts it at $5–54m.
The Zvook company says its system could cover Ukraine at 1,000 m altitude and below "for under €50 million", and that 8,000 nodes would cover the country.

observations.subject: Zvook coverage of Ukraine at 1,000 m and below
Zvook nodes needed to cover Ukraine

text: Sky Fortress covers Ukraine nationwide with no published area figure, while Zvook covered about 5% of Ukraine in 2024, on border entry routes.

metric_new.label: Share of an area covered by a sensor network

text: Sky Fortress ranges are not published; the Zvook company gives about 5 km against drones, about 6–7 km against cruise missiles and about 10 km against ballistic missiles.
Sky Fortress sends flight routes to fire teams on iPads, while Zvook sends location, direction, speed, altitude and class into Delta within about 12 seconds (company figure).
The Kyiv Post calls Ukraine's acoustic network "Sky Watch" and gives 10,000–15,000 sensors as an analysts' estimate; the rising Sky Fortress counts may also mix systems.
Zvook's drone detection range is "about 3 miles" (about 5 km) in The Telegraph and 5 km in a later trade report, and its cruise-missile range is 4 miles (about 6.4 km) against 7 km.
Zvook's 12-second figure is a company figure described both as delivery time into Delta and as "warning time", which are different measures.

In Ukraine's acoustic network, computers compare the relative strength of the engine sound across nodes to triangulate a drone's position and heading, and combining several stations gives speed and direction.
A Ukrainian defence outlet judges acoustic accuracy "significantly lower than radar", but says acoustic sensing gives a dense field at low altitude where radar is weak.
Sky Fortress phones are always recording and send over local mobile networks to a central system.
Zvook uses machine learning to class targets as helicopter, jet aircraft, cruise missile or drone.

Zvook's classifier reached about 50% accuracy in early tests; a cow's moo was once taken for a missile engine (the "cow problem"), and real missiles were sometimes classed as harmless, which the team says it fixed.

metric_new.label: Classification accuracy of a sensor or classifier

text: Missile sounds made up about 0.1% of Zvook's training data, and a distant and a close missile sound very different (the "domain shift").

observations.subject: missile sounds in Zvook training data

metric_new.label: Share of a class in training data

text: By 2026 the Zvook company claimed a false-positive rate of about 1.6%.

metric_new.label: False-positive rate of a sensor or classifier

observations.subject: Sky Fortress accuracy under Russian noise-signature changes

text: Zvook acoustic nodes are passive and emit nothing, so they do not give away their position.
Sky Fortress acoustic data is fused with radar data and sent to mobile firing teams with tablets and anti-aircraft guns.
Gen. James Hecker said that "In six hours, they teach a fighter to look at a tablet that displays the direction of the drones' movement".

observations.subject: microphones on the Russian acoustic sensor

text: No fetched source measures the effect of wind, rain or traffic noise on Ukraine's acoustic sensors, their bearing or position accuracy, or their performance against jet Gerans.
A NATO lessons-learned note (written with AI assistance, citing only press reports) lists vulnerability "to physical decoys and cyberattacks" as an open challenge for Ukraine's acoustic networks.
Soviet-era surveillance radars such as the 36D6, P-18 family, P-19 and 5N63 form Ukraine's national radar net, and many have been lost (Oryx loss list).

Ukraine's Ministry of Defence reported in June 2026 that Saab Giraffe-family radars (PS-90, PS-100, Giraffe 1X, AMB, Mk IV) sweep 360°, reach up to 100 km and 20 km altitude depending on variant, and detect "small, slow, low-altitude drones"; the Giraffe 1X is pickup-mounted, and which variants and how many are in Ukraine is not published.

observations.subject: Giraffe family altitude coverage, depending on variant

text: The Gepard's original search radar reaches up to 15 km and its S-band MPDR-18 upgrade up to 18 km; Ukraine had 40 Gepards by mid-2023, and Shaheds are "a very easy target" for them.
notes: The source's naming of the MPDR-12 and Albis radars is muddled.

text: Skynex is a radar-guided 35 mm gun battery (radar type not in fetched sources) that Parodiya decoys mislead by looking like large aircraft.
A RADA ieMHR radar costs about $1m against about $120,000 for Ukrainian analogues, by a mobile-fire-group coordinator's estimate; Oryx lists 2 RADA radars lost.

Robin Radar says a software "Long-Range Mode" for its compact, vehicle-mountable IRIS counter-drone radar, tested in Ukraine, raised detection from 5 to 12 km for drones above 180 km/h (September 2025).

observations.subject: IRIS with Long-Range Mode, drones above 180 km/h
drone speed for IRIS Long-Range Mode

text: Contra-Drone says its Ukrainian X-band CD-T10 radar detects Shaheds, FPVs and guided bombs at 15 km and up to 3 km altitude, with AI filtering out birds by radar cross-section, speed and movement; it is in test with mobile fire groups, with deliveries at the end of 2026.

Aviation expert Romanenko proposed a 30 kg vehicle radar giving each mobile fire group coordinates, speed and altitude in real time, as part of the January 2026 "anti-drone dome" of classic radars, compact radars and acoustic sensors.
Ukrainian ground radar gives poor location data for Shaheds below the horizon; a 477 km/h jet Shahed was picked up at 300 m, and some glide at 100 m.

observations.subject: jet Shahed picked up by radar

text: A Ukrainian commander said Shahed flights "at very low altitudes, up to 200 meters ... are difficult to detect by radar due to blind spots".

cites.quote: at very low altitudes, up to 200 meters ... are difficult to detect by radar due to blind spots

observations.subject: low-flying Shaheds in radar blind spots

text: Above 2 km, Shaheds "become more visible to our radars", said Ukrainian Air Force spokesman Yurii Ihnat.

cites.quote: become more visible to our radars

cites.quote: Radars cannot clearly distinguish between 3–4 simultaneous targets, showing them as one

text: Ukrainian interceptor-drone units say "We just need better radar", and that without durable, EW-protected sensors "it's very difficult".
A Kyiv mobile-defence commander wanted more over-the-horizon radar in 2025.

Deputy Air Force Commander Pavlo Yelizarov said that before spring 2026 Ukrainian units decided their own radar placement, but from spring 2026 radars are placed on a coordinated plan built from past attack patterns, moved after strikes, and their mistakes analysed.
Ukrainian mobile fire groups' thermal imaging works at night "when spotlights cannot", and is linked to the crews' shared tablet application.
Cloud cover hides drones from Ukrainian crews' thermal sights.
A Kyiv Oblast mobile-fire-group coordinator says a scope that sees about 2,000 m in clear weather sees roughly 100–200 m in rain and snow.

claimants.name: Kyiv Oblast mobile fire group coordinator

observations.subject: optical scope in rain and snow

text: Aviation expert Khrapchynskyi says low cloud, rain, snow and fog defeat visual acquisition of drones even with thermal cameras, while "Shaheds fly in any weather".
Zelensky put the fall in Ukrainian air-defence effectiveness in overcast weather at "20–30%" (October 2025).
Ukrainian helicopters carry 30 kg FLIR turrets for round-the-clock Shahed search, but attack corridors 60–70 km wide are too broad for the few helicopters.

In March 2025 the start-up Aerobavovna showed a tethered aerostat with an IR sensor under it that drops an interceptor when it sees a Shahed; the source is social-media images and no ranges are published.

A Ukrainian mobile fire group receives a drone's direction, altitude and distance, then finds it with its own observation kit, corrects for the difference between the reported and the real position, and fires only within its sector.
A Ukrainian brigade EW chief watches Russian drone links on a spectrum analyser: "I can see the flow of data in real time".

cites.quote: I can see the flow of data in real time

text: Newer Russian Gerans carry cameras and mesh radios.
Almost all Shahed-type drones aimed at Kyiv on 1–2 July 2026 used a new 3,900–4,100 MHz band, according to Serhii Beskrestnov.
A Gerbera without a modem or camera emits nothing for RF sensing to find, and no fetched source describes RF direction-finding used to track Shaheds for Ukraine's air picture.

Ukrainian air-defence crews describe a chain in which radars and other sensors are the first link and data goes through command posts to the units; each unit reports to its own combat command post, which merges information from higher command and neighbouring groups and gives orders.
Ukrainian air-defence units share a radar-based mobile app that tracks incoming attacks and is integrated with Delta; the Kyiv Independent spells it "Visage", probably Virazh.
notes: The file judges 'Visage' is probably Virazh.

text: Delta is Ukraine's cloud situational-awareness system, adopted across the forces in August 2024.

Most Ukrainian interceptions start from radar tracks, acoustic spotters and stitched feeds from Mission Control, and networked systems hand a track between crews as the target crosses sector boundaries.
Reported latencies in Ukraine's air-picture chain include ePPO report to map in 2–7 s (official) and Zvook to Delta in about 12 s (vendor); no end-to-end figure from first detection to gun was found.
A Ukrainian gunner's engagement window against a low-flying drone is "five or six seconds", and targets cross an Igla operator's sector in as little as 20 seconds.

observations.subject: gunner's engagement window at low altitude
time for a target to cross an Igla operator's sector

text: In spring 2026 the Ukrainian Air Force began tracking every drone's route across regions; before, drones that hit nothing in a region could "drop out" of its statistics, and regions had an incentive not to own drones that passed through.
One Ukrainian commander says Ukrainian SAM systems track about 10–20 targets at once.
Russia mixes drone raids with feints such as MiG take-offs, so Ukraine's air picture must be coordinated nationally.
The piston Shahed-136/Geran-2 flies at about 200 km/h (2024) or 200–210 km/h (2025).
Shahed-136/Geran-2 drones flew low (100–200 m) at first, then from 2024–25 above 2 km, cruising at 2,500–2,800 m before a near-vertical dive from 2,000–2,500 m.

The Shahed-136/Geran-2 has a two-stroke piston engine (an MD550 replica) with a "lawnmower" or moped buzz, some carry cameras, Starlink or mesh modems, and its radar return is small and better seen high than low.
The Gerbera (a decoy, scout and light-strike drone) flies at 160 km/h, holds a stable altitude when it has no modem or camera, and uses a DLE60 60 cc two-stroke Chinese hobby engine.
Some Gerberas carry a Topotek HD camera, and Gerberas with two upward/rearward cameras were seen in 2025.
A Luneburg lens makes the Gerbera look like a Shahed on radar.

The Parodiya decoy flies at a speed similar to a Shahed's, uses a DLE55RA 55 cc two-stroke engine, and carries Luneburg lenses that give it a Shahed-like radar cross-section; some devices make it mimic a large aircraft such as an Il-76.

The jet Geran-3 typically flies at 380–400 km/h, with a record of 477 km/h in March 2025 and about 300 mph (480 km/h) in another account, and had a ceiling of about 2 km in 2025; later versions carry cameras and mesh radios.
The jet Geran-4/5 flies at 350–500 km/h or 300–600 km/h depending on the source, some at 5–6 km altitude, and is heard late; a crew member said "I couldn't even see it with my eyes".

cites.quote: I couldn't even see it with my eyes

text: No fetched qualifying source gives a radar cross-section number or a measured IR signature for the Shahed, Gerbera, Parodiya or jet Gerans.
The Gerbera is built of foam over plywood; the research file infers that this gives a weak bare radar return, which is why the Luneburg lens is fitted.
notes: The weak-return point is the file's inference, not the source's.

text: A Gerbera at 160 km/h is slower than a 2025 Shahed at 200 km/h or more, which helps tell them apart, while the Parodiya flies at a Shahed-like speed and looks like one on radar.
Russian decoys can circle over a city and go back to Russia or fly on, and Gerberas fitted with extra tanks have flown over Ukraine and back.
The Ukrainian Air Force logs decoys that disappear without effect as "lost from location"; on 6–7 May 2025, 64 of 187 drones were logged that way, against 81 Shaheds shot down.

observations.subject: drones logged as lost from location

text: In early 2025 about half of radar-detected Shahed-type drones were decoys, many logged as "Lost/Fell".
Ukrainian defenders cannot be sure in time that a drone has no warhead, so they spend interceptors on decoys; Gerberas now sometimes carry about 10 kg of explosive.

claimants.name: Institute for Science and International Security

text: Decoys made up about 40% of Russian waves in May 2025, 35–40% in 2026, and "roughly one-third" in early 2026 by another account.
Serhii Beskrestnov reported in September 2025 that a Russian Supercam had been found carrying a radio-signal detector that makes it evade, often by diving, when it senses a transmission.
Shaheds fly faster and lower than Russian observation drones, which helps tell them apart on a track.

mentions.name: Russian fixed-wing ISR drones (Orlan, Zala, Supercam)

text: In 2023 Russian Tu-95 strike packages used Shaheds as pathfinders to find gaps in Ukrainian air defence (RUSI).

Russian waves of 5–10 Shaheds come in from one sector at different altitudes; a Ukrainian commander says "There are only two goals: overload the Ukrainian air defense system and identify positions", and decoys map radar coverage by altitude.

cites.quote: There are only two goals: overload the Ukrainian air defense system and identify positions

text: Russian decoys reveal Ukrainian air-defence, radar and EW positions for later strikes.

claimants.name: Institute for Science and International Security

text: A Ukrainian air-defence officer said of Russian drone raids in 2026: "They're probing, feeling things out".

In 2025 a Kyiv mobile-fire-group commander said some Shaheds "react to light", manoeuvring when the searchlights come on, some are "steered online", and they "film our positions ... so later they try to fly around us".

cites.quote: film our positions ... so later they try to fly around us

text: In April 2026 Serhii Beskrestnov reported "another hit by a guided Shahed on a mobile fire group crew. The group was working on one drone, while another at that moment was hunting the crew".

cites.quote: another hit by a guided Shahed on a mobile fire group crew

text: A Lancet hit the TRML-4D radar of an IRIS-T SLM in a video of June 2023; the damage is unclear, but the truck stayed immobile afterwards, and "radars are notoriously fragile".
When Ukraine pushed air defence forward, Russia found it and struck it, usually with 9M723 Iskanders (RUSI).

Oryx had visually confirmed, as of 18 November 2026, 152 Ukrainian radars and communications systems lost: 113 destroyed, 24 damaged, 1 abandoned and 14 captured; Oryx does not attribute causes in this list.

Ukrainian radar losses visually confirmed by Oryx include 16 36D6 "Tin Shield", 16 36D6 ST-68U, 14 P-18 "Malakhit", 12 P-18, 4 P-18ML, 16 5N63S (S-300PS), 2 TRML-4D, 2 AN/MPQ-53, 1 AN/MPQ-64 Sentinel, 2 RADA ieMHR and 1 MR-18.
notes: The summary (12/0005) gives 16 36D6 and 18 P-18-family; this detailed list gives 32 36D6 and 30 P-18-family.

text: Oryx has visually confirmed 51 Ukrainian self-propelled anti-aircraft guns lost, including 1 Gepard.

In autumn 2022 the first Russian Shahed waves came low and at night, against Ukrainian radars with blind zones; ePPO launched on 13 October, Zvook fielded its first 40 stations, and mobile fire groups listened for drones.

In 2023 to mid-2024 Russian Shahed waves grew, Shaheds served as pathfinders for missile packages and Lancets hit radars, while Ukraine's acoustic net grew to 6,000–9,500 nodes with tablets for fire teams, alongside Gepard radars.

From late 2024 to March 2025 Russia added Gerbera and Parodiya decoys with Luneburg lenses (from July 2024) and the jet Geran-3, so Ukrainian radar operators had to judge Shahed or decoy; ePPO had 200,000 active users.

In 2025 Russian Shaheds flew above 2 km and in low blind spots, camera Shaheds avoided searchlights, about 40% of drones were decoys and weather was exploited; Ukraine fielded 14,000 Sky Fortress nodes, the IRIS radar's long-range mode and a Delta-linked air-picture app.

In 2026 guided Shaheds hunted Ukrainian mobile fire groups and jet Gerans flew at 5–6 km and were heard late, using mesh radios and new bands; Ukraine answered with coordinated radar siting, route tracking across regions, CD-T10 radars with mobile fire groups, the "anti-drone dome" and Giraffe radars.
